body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Dental caries in children after cessation of community water fluoridation: a comparison of two cities","authors":"Brannigan-Oyelowo S, Lindqvist-Amadi P, Ferro-Mackenzie T","year":2018,"venue":"Community Oral Health Research","doi":"10.5555/cohr.2018.0092","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We compared dental caries in children aged 7 to 10 in a city that stopped community water fluoridation with a city that continued it, using school dental examinations before and five years after cessation. Decay-affected surfaces rose by 0.7 per child in the city that stopped, with no change in the comparison city. The increase was largest in children eligible for free school meals. The two cities differed in dental service provision, and examiners were not blinded to city. Dental attendance fell slightly in both cities over the period."},{"title":"Public attitudes to community water fluoridation: a qualitative study of a contested local decision","authors":"Okonjo-Harding L, Silvestri-Mbeki A","year":2021,"venue":"Health Policy and Society","doi":"10.5555/hps.2021.0215","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We interviewed 36 residents, councillors and health professionals in a town that debated ending fluoridation. Views on fluoridation were shaped more by trust in the council and in experts than by evidence about teeth. Opponents framed fluoridation as a question of choice and consent; supporters framed it as fairness for children who do not see a dentist. Both sides described the consultation as adversarial. Parents with young children were under-represented, and no interviews were held in languages other than English."},{"title":"Parents' knowledge of fluoridation status and use of fluoride toothpaste: a cross-sectional survey","authors":"Varga-Collins H, Ndlovu-Pearce J","year":2016,"venue":"Journal of Child Oral Health","doi":"10.5555/jcoh.2016.0147","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We surveyed 1,212 parents of children under five in three areas with different fluoridation histories. Only 38 percent of parents knew whether their water was fluoridated, and knowledge was lowest in the most deprived areas. Parents who knew their water was not fluoridated were no more likely to use fluoride toothpaste of adequate strength. Most parents took advice on toothpaste from pharmacies and supermarkets rather than from dental teams. Response was lower in deprived areas. The authors recommend telling families directly when the fluoridation status of their water changes."},{"title":"Dentists' responses to the end of water fluoridation: interviews in general dental practice","authors":"Achterberg-Nwosu F, Delacroix-Owen M","year":2023,"venue":"Primary Dental Care Research","doi":"10.5555/pdcr.2023.0061","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We interviewed 22 dentists and dental nurses in practices serving a town where fluoridation had recently ended. Participants described increasing fluoride varnish for young children but lacked appointments to reach families who did not attend. Several felt that public health teams had left them to explain the decision to parents without support. Participants disagreed about whether to raise fluoridation with parents at all. Most practices had long waiting lists for new child patients. Some participants had stopped mentioning fluoridation to avoid arguments with parents."},{"title":"Inequalities in child dental extractions after fluoridation cessation: an interrupted time series","authors":"Rahimi-Carlsen J, Obuya-Fletcher N","year":2019,"venue":"Community Oral Health Research","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We used hospital records of dental extractions under general anaesthesia in children for eight years around the end of fluoridation in one region. Extraction rates rose after cessation, with the largest increase in the most deprived quintile (rate ratio 1.46) and little change in the least deprived quintile (rate ratio 1.05). A concurrent change in the referral pathway may explain part of the rise. Extractions are a late and severe outcome and miss most decay. The authors call for earlier measures of decay, such as school examinations, to monitor the effects of cessation."},{"title":"Misinformation and trust in local fluoridation debates: content analysis of public consultation responses","authors":"Hallorann-Ito K, Mensah-Duarte R, Lindgren-Okafor B","year":2024,"venue":"Health Communication Studies","doi":"10.5555/hcs.2024.0039","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed 1,960 written responses to a council consultation on community water fluoridation. In all, 42 percent of responses cited health fears not supported by the evidence reviewed by the council, and 27 percent questioned the council's honesty rather than the science. Responses in favour of fluoridation were shorter and more often cited children's teeth. Few responses came from parents of young children or from people in the most deprived neighbourhoods. The authors recommend engagement that starts from trust, not from correcting facts."},{"title":"Community engagement methods for contested public health decisions: a scoping review","authors":"Petrakis-Oduya E, Blom-Sinclair T","year":2020,"venue":"Public Health Methods Reviews","doi":"10.5555/phmr.2020.0104","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We mapped methods used to engage communities in contested public health decisions such as fluoridation, vaccination programmes and speed limits. We included 31 studies. Deliberative methods, such as citizens' panels, reached a broader range of residents than open consultations, which were dominated by organised groups. Few studies evaluated whether engagement changed decisions or trust. Studies rarely reported how they reached people with low literacy or limited English. The authors suggest planning engagement before a decision is framed, with explicit steps to reach residents who do not usually respond to consultations."}]}
